issues.explanation: 'I dwell on how the event could have been prevented' can occur after accidents, but here the rest of the profile centers on sensory trauma cues and intrusive memory/avoidance rather than a coherent prevention-focused appraisal pattern. With Negative Appraisals absent and no threat/appraisal content linking to preventability, this strategy feels weakly grounded relative to the formulation and selected items.

vignette: Dr. Luis Hernandez, a 62-year-old Latin American surgeon, had always taken pride in his ability to remain calm and composed under pressure. But that all changed one fateful night when he was involved in a severe car accident on his way home from a late-night surgery shift. The crash left him with multiple injuries, including a badly broken leg and a deep gash on his forehead. As Luis recovered in the hospital, memories of the accident flooded his mind, feeling more real and vivid than any ordinary memory. He could recall the sound of screeching tires, the crunching of metal, and the eerie feeling of weightlessness as his car spun out of control. The image of his mangled car door, twisted beyond recognition, haunted him like a ghostly apparition. The memories came unbidden, forcing their way into his mind when he least expected it - while scrubbing in for surgery, during quiet moments with his wife, even in the shower. Luis found himself pushing these memories away before he could fully recall them, as if trying to prevent himself from being overwhelmed by the sheer intensity of the experience. But avoidance became a pattern in other areas of his life too. He stopped taking long drives on weekends, fearing another accident; gave up playing tennis with friends, worried about putting excessive stress on his still-healing leg; and avoided talking about the accident altogether, fearing it would trigger more memories he couldn't control. His wife, Maria, noticed the change in him - how withdrawn he'd become, how reluctant to engage in activities they used to enjoy together. Even tactile sensations triggered memories of the crash: the feeling of rough fabric against his skin made him think of the hospital gown he wore for weeks after the accident; a specific texture on his car's steering wheel brought back the sensation of gripping it tightly as his car careened out of control. The sight of cars involved in accidents, even minor fender-benders, filled him with an inexplicable dread. Luis tried to push through these feelings, telling himself he was a surgeon - trained to remain calm under pressure - but the images lingered. His work suffered too; during operations, his usual steady hands would tremble ever so slightly when he had to navigate tight spaces or manipulate delicate tissue. Colleagues began to notice his mistakes, and though they were minor, Luis knew it was only a matter of time before something more serious happened. It wasn't until one particularly harrowing surgery session - where Luis's hands shook uncontrollably as he tried to repair a damaged artery - that he realized he needed help. The feeling of being completely out of control had finally become too much to bear, and with Maria's encouragement, Luis sought therapy for the first time in his life. Now, as he sat in Dr. Rodriguez's office, Luis couldn't shake off the fear that he'd never regain his composure, that these memories would forever define him. He hoped that somehow, someway, therapy could help him tame the ghosts of that fateful night and reclaim his sense of self - both in the operating room and out.
